passage: Recess was only ten minutes today because of the assembly, and Akash was picking the kho-kho team fast. "You, you, you." He skipped right past Tsering, the new boy whose family had come from Darjeeling. "Not him, he talks funny." A few kids laughed. Aparna felt her face go hot. Tsering looked down at his shoes. passage: Every evening the boys and girls of Sunrise Apartments played cricket in the parking lot. passage:
I'm Lalit, ten, the smallest boy in our colony's cricket gang. Last summer something happened in our colony that I still think about.
Santosh's family had just moved from another state, and at home they speak a different language. He sat on the wall every evening watching us play cricket. Nobody picked him. When he asked, one of the older boys said, "You're not from here. Go play with your own people." Some kids laughed.
My stomach felt twisted. Santosh wasn't even my friend yet. But it just wasn't fair. He lives here now, same as us.
I said, "That's not fair. He can bat after me." My voice shook a bit. The older boy rolled his eyes, but he let him.
Santosh hit a four on his first ball. After that, nobody said anything. Now he's on my team every evening.

qa.q: What did Santosh hit on his first ball?
qa.a: He hit a four.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling when he spoke up, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt it was unfair and was a little nervous, since his stomach twisted and his voice shook, but he still spoke.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the game, and what did Lalit's choice change?
qa.a: When Lalit said Santosh could bat after him, the older boy let him play, and Santosh became part of the team.

qa.q: How might Santosh have felt sitting on the wall before Lalit spoke up?
qa.a: He probably felt left out and lonely, watching the game every evening in a new place where nobody picked him.

grounding: It shows a child who objects when a boy from another community is left out of a game, caring about fairness even for someone who is not yet his friend.

passage:
PE note, Tuesday. Jahnavi, games teacher, Class 5.
Mira joined us this term; her family runs the travelling fair and she will be with us for two months. In today's handball game, her team kept passing around her. When she called for the ball, one girl said, "She's only here for a bit, why bother?"
Tejas, who is on the other team and barely knows Mira, stopped playing and walked over to me. His ears were red. He said, "Ma'am, that's not fair. She's in our class too. Two months is still our class."
I blew the whistle and changed the rule: everyone must touch the ball before a goal counts. Mira scored the next goal.
Next: I will talk with the class about being fair to every classmate, and thank Tejas privately for speaking up.

qa.q: What rule did Jahnavi add to the game?
qa.a: Everyone must touch the ball before a goal counts.

qa.q: What does Tejas's red face suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt nervous or upset but strongly that leaving Mira out was wrong, enough to stop playing and speak up.

qa.q: Which choice by Tejas made a difference, and why?
qa.a: Walking over to tell the teacher it was unfair, even though Mira isn't his friend, led to a rule change that included her.

qa.q: How might Mira have felt when her team kept passing around her?
qa.a: Mira probably felt left out and unwanted, as if being new and short-term meant she did not count.

grounding: It shows a child who objects when a classmate from another community is left out of the game, showing concern for fairness beyond his friends.

In the village near Kurnool, the evening kho-kho game was starting in the temple ground. Vinita, nine, stood at the edge. She lived in the houses across the stream.
"Not her," said Ravi, the captain. "My mother says we don't play with them."
A few children laughed. Vinita looked at her feet.
Suraj, ten, felt something hot rise in his chest. He had heard adults say things like that too, but it had never looked so ugly.
"That's not fair," he said. "She runs faster than you."
"Mind your business."
"It is my business. If she doesn't play, I don't play."
There was a pause. Two others moved to stand next to Suraj. Ravi scowled, then shrugged. "Fine. She's on your team."
Vinita tagged three people in the first round.

qa.q: How many people did Vinita tag in the first round?
qa.a: Three people.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when Ravi said "Not her"?
qa.a: He felt angry and uncomfortable, sensing it was unfair to leave Vinita out.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Suraj saying it was unfair and refusing to play without Vinita worked, because others joined him and the captain gave way.

qa.q: What was it like for Vinita at the edge of the game?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed, looking at her feet while others laughed.

grounding: It shows a child objecting when a classmate from another community is left out of a game, showing fairness beyond friends.

The football game in the schoolyard in São Paulo was about to begin. Ines, nine, had arrived from Bolivia only a month ago. She stood by the fence, hands in her pockets.
"She can't play," said Lucas. "She doesn't even speak properly."
Some kids laughed at her accent.
Priscila, nine, had never really talked to Ines. But her face went hot.
"That's not fair," she said. "Everyone plays at break. That's the rule."
"She's not one of us."
"She's in our class. That makes her one of us."
Priscila walked over to Ines. "Do you want to play?"
Ines nodded slowly.
"She's on my team," Priscila said.
Ines scored in the first ten minutes. Lucas didn't say anything else.

qa.a: She felt angry and embarrassed for Ines, even though they weren't friends.

qa.a: She named the unfairness, reminded everyone of the rule and personally invited Ines onto her team.

qa.a: She probably felt relieved and welcomed after standing alone by the fence.

At the summer camp in Pune, the cricket teams were picked by the camp leaders' favourites. Arnab, eleven, had come from Kolkata. He spoke Hindi slowly, and every day he was picked last.
Today, nobody picked him at all.
"He can't even understand what we say," one boy muttered. "Let him sit."
Anjali, eleven, was captain of the second team. She didn't know Arnab well. But she remembered her own first week, when nobody sat with her.
"That's not fair," she said to the camp leader. "Everyone should play."
"There are enough players."
"Then I'll sit out and he can take my place."
The camp leader looked at her, then changed the rule: teams would be chosen by drawing names from now on.
Arnab batted fourth and hit two boundaries.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when nobody picked Arnab?
qa.a: She felt upset and uncomfortable, remembering her own lonely first week and sensing it was unfair.

qa.q: What did Anjali do, and why did it work?
qa.a: She told the camp leader it was unfair and offered her own place, which led the leader to change the rule for everyone.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt being left standing every day?
qa.a: He probably felt lonely and rejected, especially when nobody picked him at all.

The school sports period was cut to twenty minutes because of the heat, and everyone rushed to form relay teams. Chandrika, ten, saw that Ankita, whose family had just moved from Bihar and who spoke Bhojpuri at home, was standing alone again.
"We only have time for fast people," one of the girls said.
